claims.text: Fine coherent nanoprecipitates govern high-temperature plastic strain in refractory compositionally complex alloys.
Fine coherent nanoprecipitates govern high-temperature toughness in refractory compositionally complex alloys.
Precipitation-induced barriers increase strain hardening and strength.
Coherent precipitate interfaces provide pathways for dislocation transmission or transfer.
Coherent precipitate interfaces facilitate crack-tip blunting.
Progressive strain hardening caused by nanoprecipitation delays localized plastic instability.
Crack-tip blunting at coherent precipitate interfaces delays crack propagation.
A post-processing aging treatment can induce stepwise, controllable coherent nanoprecipitation in the refractory alloy.
The relevant nanoprecipitates will remain fine, coherent, stable, and uniformly distributed in the matrix under the stated high-temperature conditions.
Temperatures from approximately 800 to 1000 °C are typical of fusion plasma-facing service.
The aged alloy containing coherent nanoprecipitates will have higher high-temperature yield strength than the baseline.
The aged alloy containing coherent nanoprecipitates will sustain greater plastic strain before failure than the baseline.
The aged alloy containing coherent nanoprecipitates will have improved high-temperature fracture toughness relative to the baseline.
Coarser precipitates or an increased hard-phase fraction can reduce plastic strain.
The proposed mechanism is valid mainly between approximately 800 and 1000 °C in high-melting-point alloys with stable single-phase microstructures.

contradictions.description: The boundary invokes stable single-phase microstructures, whereas the hypothesized operative state contains a distinct population of nanoprecipitates and is therefore not strictly single-phase.
